samples.summary: Repeated `?state=` on the GitHub callback makes `stateToken.startsWith` throw a TypeError (500) instead of a graceful refusal
samples.evidence: `verifyCallbackState` does `stateToken?.startsWith(WEB_STATE_PREFIX)`. `@Query('state')` is typed `string | undefined` but Express yields an *array* for `?state=a&state=b`, and `Array.prototype.startsWith` does not exist → TypeError, which escapes the `catch` (it only special-cases `UnauthorizedException`) and surfaces as an unhandled 500. The previous code did `this.cliAuthStore.consumeState(stateToken)` (a `Map.get`, safe for any value) and then threw a clean `BadRequestException`, so this is a new crash path introduced by the change. Reachability is limited (the passport guard must first succeed, i.e. a genuine GitHub `code`), hence medium confidence, but a normalizing guard (`typeof stateToken === 'string'`) costs one line.

samples.summary: A non-matching callback clears the whole flow cookie, cancelling the other concurrent logins the binding ring exists to support
samples.evidence: In `takeStateCookie`, when `hit === undefined` the code sets `remaining = []` and unconditionally calls `res.clearCookie(name, options)`. Concrete user path: two login tabs give cookie `[A, B]`; tab A completes (cookie becomes `[B]`); the user then presses Back / refreshes the callback URL, replaying `state = sig(A)`. Nothing matches, so the cookie is cleared and tab B's still-pending login is now unverifiable — it will be bounced to `/login?error=login_state`. That is exactly the invisible failure `MAX_CONCURRENT_LOGINS` was added to prevent, re-introduced on the replay path. The doc comment acknowledges the trade-off, but a browser refresh of the callback URL is not a rare 'bogus callback'.

samples.summary: Concurrent headless `wafflebase login` runs share one `login-url.txt`; the first to settle deletes the second's still-live URL
samples.evidence: `announceLoginUrl` writes to a fixed path `join(dirname(getConfigPath()), 'login-url.txt')` and `rmSync(file, { force: true })`s it first. Two non-TTY logins on the same machine: the second run overwrites the first's URL (the first user's printed path now yields the wrong login), and whichever run reaches its `finally` first (`login.ts:82`) deletes the file out from under the other, which is still waiting on its callback. Nothing keys the file to the process/nonce (e.g. a pid- or token-suffixed name).

samples.summary: CLI now blocks a terminal for the full 5 minutes on server-side refusals it could detect immediately
samples.evidence: `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS` was raised 30s → 5 min, and the timer starts at `startCallbackServer(nonce)` (line 52-53), before the browser is even launched. If the backend refuses the start outright — e.g. `cliLoginAvailable` false → `BadRequestException('Command-line sign-in requires an https server')` (github-auth.guard.ts:441-445), or any 400 for a missing nonce/challenge — the browser shows the error but the CLI has no signal at all and sits for 300s before printing 'Login timed out'. The same applies to the `sawUnboundCode` branch (line 466): the CLI already *knows* at that instant the callback was unbound, yet defers the message to the timeout. The window is also strictly out of phase with the server's, whose 5-minute state TTL starts at the consent click, not at server start.

samples.summary: `githubAuth` takes `@Res()` but sends nothing on the non-consent path, so any guard outcome that resolves `true` hangs the request
samples.evidence: The handler now declares `@Res() res: Response` and only writes a response inside `if (consent)`. Using `@Res()` disables Nest's automatic response, so if `GitHubAuthGuard.canActivate` ever resolves `true` without passport having redirected (the guard's own `return true` is the consent case, but `super.canActivate` resolving `true` is not structurally excluded), the socket is left open until a proxy/client timeout. Before this change the handler had no `@Res()`, so Nest would have terminated the request with an empty 200. Low confidence on reachability with passport-oauth2, but the failure mode changed from 'empty response' to 'hung request'.

samples.summary: `process.exit()` immediately after `console.error` can truncate the error envelope on a piped stderr — the exact agent-harness case the envelope targets
samples.evidence: `failFromBackend` does `console.error(backendErrorEnvelope(...))` then `return process.exit(...)`. When stderr is a pipe (not a TTY), Node's writes are asynchronous and `process.exit` does not flush pending buffered data, so the single-line envelope this change exists to guarantee can be lost precisely when the consumer is a harness reading a pipe. Setting `process.exitCode` and returning, or awaiting a drain, avoids it.

samples.summary: A 200 response with no bytes is reported as `HTTP 200`, which reads as a success
samples.evidence: `if (!res.ok || !res.bytes)` funnels both failures into `backendErrorEnvelope(res.data, { code: 'HTTP_ERROR', message: `HTTP ${res.status}` }, command)`. For the `res.ok && !res.bytes` half that emits `{"error":{"code":"HTTP_ERROR","message":"HTTP 200"}}`. Previously the message was simply absent, so nothing was misleading; now the envelope actively asserts a 200 as the error reason. The empty-body case needs its own code/message.

samples.summary: `runCli` registers a fresh `preAction` hook on every invocation of a caller-supplied program
samples.evidence: `program.hook('preAction', ...)` is called unconditionally at the top of `runCli`. With the default argument a new program is built each time, but `runCli(program, argv)` with a reused program (as tests do) accumulates one hook per call on the same `Command`. The hooks are idempotent in effect (they all assign `acting`), so this is cosmetic, but it grows unboundedly if `runCli` is ever driven in a loop.

finding.summary: `secureCookies` still returns true for `NODE_ENV=production` regardless of scheme, so a production image served over plain http sets `Secure`/`__Host-` login cookies the browser discards — browser login dead-ends and the CLI consent page loops forever
finding.evidence: `function secureCookies(configService) { if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') return true; const callbackUrl = ...startsWith('https://'); }`. The OR with NODE_ENV contradicts the stated rule (`docs/design/backend.md:384`: "it is not keyed to `NODE_ENV`: it applies whenever `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL` is `https://`"). `Dockerfile:88` sets `ENV NODE_ENV=production`, and `packages/documentation/developers/self-hosting.md:42` / `README.md:126` document `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://localhost:3000/auth/github/callback`. On that combination `loginCookieName` yields `__Host-…` and `loginCookieOptions.secure=true`; browsers reject `Secure`/`__Host-` cookies from an http origin, so (a) `verifyCallbackState`'s web branch never finds `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` and every callback redirects to `/login?error=login_state`, and (b) `GitHubAuthGuard.hasConfirmation` never sees `wafflebase_cli_confirm`, so clicking Continue on the consent page just re-renders a fresh consent page — an unbreakable loop with no error text. Making the check scheme-first (or `secureCookies = https-callback || (production && !http-callback)`) avoids it.

verdict.reason: The quoted code does not exist. `secureCookies` (packages/backend/src/auth/github-auth.guard.ts:91-98) is already scheme-first — exactly the fix the finding proposes: it lowercases `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL`, returns true on `https://` (line 95), returns FALSE on `http://` (line 96), and only falls back to `process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production'` (line 97) when no callback URL is configured/parseable. There is no leading `if (process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production') return true;` and no OR with NODE_ENV. Grep for `NODE_ENV === 'production'` across packages/backend/src returns only guard line 97 (plus unrelated app.module.ts:87), and `secureCookies` has one definition, consumed by auth.controller.ts:35/528. On the exact scenario claimed (Dockerfile NODE_ENV=production + documented `GITHUB_CALLBACK_URL=http://localhost:3000/auth/github/callback`), line 96 returns false, so `loginCookieName` (line 165) yields the bare cookie name and `loginCookieOptions.secure` (line 176) is false — no Secure/`__Host-` cookie is emitted on the http origin, so neither the `/login?error=login_state` dead-end nor the CLI consent loop can arise. The design doc rule (docs/design/backend.md:371-378) matches the implementation, and github-auth.guard.spec.ts:675-695 is an explicit regression test for the http-callback-with-NODE_ENV=production combination.

finding.summary: Two concurrent CLI logins (or two concurrent browser logins) in one browser collide on the single-named state/confirm cookies: the second start overwrites the first's binding and the first callback is refused as a forgery
finding.evidence: `browserBinding: this.issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_STATE_COOKIE)` writes the fixed name `wafflebase_cli_state`; `issueLoginCookie(context, CLI_CONFIRM_COOKIE)` likewise, and the browser flow writes the fixed `OAUTH_STATE_COOKIE` at line 360. The comment at github-auth.guard.ts:22-29 argues separate names are needed precisely because "one shared name means the second start overwrites the first's binding and the first callback is refused as a forgery, which is a login that fails for a reason no one can see" — but that reasoning applies unchanged to two `wafflebase login` runs, or to a user opening the login page in two tabs. `verifyCallbackState` (auth.controller.ts:314-328) then throws BadRequestException for the first CLI callback and its CLI waits out the full 5-minute `CALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS`; the browser case redirects to `/login?error=login_state`. Nothing keys the cookie name (or a map inside one cookie) to the individual login.

verdict.reason: The claimed mechanism does not exist in the code. `issueLoginCookie` (github-auth.guard.ts:570-589) appends the new binding to the existing cookie value instead of overwriting it: it reads `loginCookieValues(req?.cookies?.[name])`, keeps the last MAX_CONCURRENT_LOGINS-1 entries, and writes `joinLoginCookieValues([...kept, value])`. MAX_CONCURRENT_LOGINS=3 with a `.` separator over base64url values (github-auth.guard.ts:193-211). On the callback side, `takeStateCookie` (auth.controller.ts:356-378) searches all values (`values.find(matches)`) and spends only the matched one, re-setting the remainder, and both the browser (auth.controller.ts:303-305) and CLI (auth.controller.ts:316-318) branches of `verifyCallbackState` use it. The CLI confirm cookie is handled the same way (`matchedConfirmation` at github-auth.guard.ts:534-549, `spendLoginCookie` at 595-618). `req.cookies` is populated at guard time because cookie-parser is global middleware (main.ts:64), so the append reads real prior values. Therefore two concurrent CLI logins, or two browser tabs, each retain their own binding and neither callback is refused as a forgery. Only >3 simultaneous logins of one flow evict the oldest, which is a different, documented tradeoff and not the claim made.

finding.summary: The single-use `/launch/<token>` redirect has no recovery path: any consumer other than the user's browser (link scanner, prefetch, opener probe, a second window) burns the token and the real browser gets a bare 404
finding.evidence: `launchTarget = undefined;` after the first successful GET means a second request to the same URL falls into the `!launchTarget` branch and returns `res.writeHead(404); res.end('Not found')`. The user has no way to retry — the authorization URL is only in the (owner-only) `login-url.txt` on non-TTY stderr, and on a TTY it was printed before the hop, so a TTY user who loses the race sees only a 404 page and then a five-minute wait. Given the URL is handed to an arbitrary system opener (`openBrowser`), a duplicate dereference is not far-fetched.

verdict.reason: The described code does not exist in this tree. A second visit to the spent `/launch/<token>` link is caught at login.ts:432-440 by `if (isOurToken) { res.writeHead(410, ...); res.end(SPENT_LAUNCH_PAGE); }`, which returns a page (login.ts:314-341) that explicitly names the remedy: "Return to your terminal, press Ctrl-C, and run `wafflebase login` again." The bare `res.writeHead(404); res.end('Not found')` at login.ts:443-444 is reached only when `isOurToken` is false (an unknown/guessed token), never for the real browser holding the issued link, because `armLaunch` (login.ts:551-555) sets `launchToken` and `launchTarget` together before the URL is handed out and `nonceMatches` (login.ts:297-302) matches the issued token regardless of whether the target was already spent. Both the claimed evidence (404 on second visit) and the claimed consequence (no recovery path, forced five-minute wait) are contradicted by the code.
